title: The Fed May Raise Rates Again — And the Rupee Is Already Feeling the Heat
excerpt: With US inflation at 3.8% and the rupee at record lows near 97/$, NRIs face a double squeeze on remittances, mortgages, and investments
body:
The spectre of a Federal Reserve rate hike — the first in over three years — is no longer a fringe forecast. It is rapidly becoming the market's base case, and for the estimated 18 million Indians living abroad, the implications are immediate and deeply personal.

Minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee's April 28-29 meeting, released last week, revealed an institution consumed by inflation anxiety. US consumer prices rose 3.8 per cent in April, the highest annual rate since May 2023, while wholesale inflation surged to a blistering 6 per cent — the sharpest jump since December 2022. The Iran war, which disrupted energy exports through the Strait of Hormuz beginning in late February, has sent crude prices above $111 per barrel, triggering cost increases that have rippled far beyond the petrol pump.

Three FOMC members — Beth Hammack, Neel Kashkari, and Lorie Logan — refused to endorse language suggesting the Fed's next move would be a rate cut. They wanted the statement to acknowledge that a hike was equally likely. Market pricing now assigns a 60 per cent probability to a 25-basis-point increase by January, with December odds sitting at roughly a coin flip.

## Warsh Inherits a Minefield

Kevin Warsh, who was sworn in as Fed Chair on Friday after Jerome Powell's departure, enters office with a fundamental contradiction. Both Warsh and President Trump have advocated for lower interest rates, but the inflation data leaves precious little room for cuts. "I'm going to let him do what he wants to do," Trump told reporters — but what Warsh may *need* to do could be the opposite of what either man wanted.

The real economy is already responding. Mortgage rates have climbed 35 basis points in the past three months. "Inflation is now running higher than wage growth, so homebuyers are losing real purchasing power with each coming CPI readout," notes Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com. For the hundreds of thousands of Indian-Americans who bought homes in the 2020-2024 period with adjustable-rate mortgages, the squeeze is beginning to bite.

## The Rupee's Parallel Crisis

Half a world away, the Indian rupee has been caught in the same vortex. The currency slid to a record low of 96.25 against the dollar on Monday, having lost 5.5 per cent since the Iran conflict erupted — making it Asia's worst-performing currency in 2026. DBS Group Research has raised its forecast range to 95-100 for the remainder of the year, while some analysts warn the psychologically devastating 100-per-dollar mark could be breached if the RBI fails to announce measures to improve dollar inflows.

India imports roughly 80-85 per cent of its crude oil. At $111 per barrel, the country's oil marketing companies must purchase vastly more dollars to settle import invoices, draining rupee liquidity and creating structural downward pressure on the exchange rate. Foreign investors have net sold over $23.5 billion in Indian stocks and bonds since March, accelerating the capital flight.

Emkay Global has warned that even an RBI rate hike would be an "imperfect defence" for the currency. "Rate hikes serve as a fire extinguisher to a volcano," the brokerage noted, drawing parallels with 2013, when emergency tightening measures backfired as the rupee still fell nearly 15 per cent in seven weeks.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs, the macro picture creates a paradox. A stronger dollar means each remittance converts into more rupees — families receiving monthly transfers from the US, UK, or Gulf are temporarily better off. But the other side of that coin is brutal: rising US interest rates make mortgages, car loans, and credit card debt more expensive in the countries where NRIs actually live and work.

Indian real estate investments, a perennial favourite among the diaspora, face a double hit. While property prices in rupee terms may continue rising, the dollar-denominated return has been eroding fast. An NRI who invested ₹1 crore in a Bangalore flat in January 2026 has already seen its dollar value fall by roughly 5.5 per cent, purely from currency depreciation.

The investment calculus is shifting. With US Treasury yields potentially heading toward 5 per cent or higher, the risk premium required to justify parking capital in Indian markets has increased substantially. "Growth risks dampen prospects for any reversal in equity inflows, while low carry, high hedging costs, concerns around wider fiscal deficit and rate hikes would reduce scope for debt flows," analysts at Bank of America warned.

## Looking Ahead

The next inflection point arrives with the May CPI data, due in mid-June. If headline inflation ticks above 4 per cent or core inflation remains sticky at 2.8 per cent, the June FOMC meeting under Warsh's stewardship could mark the beginning of a tightening cycle that markets have not priced for since 2023. For the diaspora, it is a moment to revisit financial plans — from remittance timing to mortgage structures to the allocation between Indian and dollar-denominated assets.
